newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel opposes date to end German solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: Waigel opposes date to end German solidarity tax.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday he was against setting a concrete date to repeal the controversial "solidarity surcharge tax" that helps to pay for German unification.

Waigel told the Berlin radio station Hundert 6 that demands to set a firm date to do away with the tax were unfounded because proposals to make up for the expected 16 billion marks in lost annual revenues have not yet been put forward.
Waigel said the solidarity tax, brought in after unification to help rebuild east Germany's battered economy, must be reduced in stages before being fully repealed.
He noted the deal reached in late December to cut the tax surcharge by two points from from January 1998 to 5.5 percent was an initial step at reducing the burden on taxpayers.

The Free Democratic Party (FDP), junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 14-year ruling coalition led by his Christian Democrats (CDU), has demanded that the unpopular tax be repealed by January 2000.

Reducing the tax has been a sore point between the FDP, which has staked its political fate on tax cuts, and Kohl's CDU, which has been keen to bolster state revenues ahead of European monetary union beginning in January 1999.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms told the Magdeburg newspaper "Volkstimme am Sonntag" at the weekend reiterated the FDP view that the tax must be repealed by 2000.
